The money shot — full moon rising behind a skyline — needs the rise time, the transit and the azimuth sense together. This tool's transit tells you when the Moon crosses the meridian, highest and due south (or north).
Moon overhead and underfoot periods anchor solunar lore; tides themselves follow the Moon's transit more than its face. The times here are the ones the lore is computed from.
Some dates have no moonrise at all — the Moon's daily ~50-minute slip means one calendar day a month gets skipped for each event. The tool reports the gap instead of forcing a time.

Near the autumn equinox at mid-northern latitudes, moonrise comes only about 25–30 minutes later on successive evenings instead of the usual ~50 — the shallow ecliptic angle at work, and the reason harvest moons feel glued to sunset.

At first quarter the Moon transits near sunset, rises around midday and sets around midnight; at last quarter it rises around midnight and transits near dawn. The phase name alone predicts the shift pattern — the calculator fills in the minutes.

faq: Why is there no moonrise on my date?

About once a month for each event: the Moon's ~50-minute daily delay pushes a rise past midnight, so one calendar date gets none and the next gets a very early one. It is the calendar's edge, not missing data.
The underlying model is a truncated lunar theory sampled at five-minute intervals — fine for planning, typically within 10–20 minutes of almanac values. Almanac-grade work uses full ephemerides.
What is upper transit good for?

Transit is the Moon's highest point — best altitude for observing, and the reference moment around which rise and set arrange themselves. Anglers' solunar major periods key off transits (and the opposite, lower transit).
Why do rise times jump around near the poles?
At high latitudes the Moon can stay up (or down) for days around its declination extremes — the lunar version of polar day. Missing events there are geometry, reported honestly.
Does the Moon rise exactly in the east?

Only near the equinoxes. Its rising point swings along the horizon with its declination — up to ±28.6° of latitude worth of swing, wider than the Sun's. The compass point varies monthly, which ruin-alignment hunters know well.

Event definitions use the Moon's upper limb at the horizon with standard refraction, the almanac convention — the same care the sunrise definition takes, applied to a moving target with parallax, which the model handles approximately.
Can I get times for a whole month?
Day by day here; the Moon Phase Calendar Map gives the month's phases alongside, and pairing the two — phase for the what, this page for the when — covers a month of planning.
